motivation: Popular and practitioner commentary portrays Generation Z as unusually ethics-driven at work, yet peer-reviewed generational research finds small or inconsistent cohort differences in work values. A sharper question is not whether Gen Z is 'more ethical' but how ethical concerns get expressed, and through which channel, once an employer's ethical commitments are seen as broken.
problem: When employees perceive that their organization has failed to honour its ethical commitments, what determines whether they raise the concern internally, take it public, leave quietly, or stay silent; and is the apparent Gen Z tendency toward public rather than internal voice a cohort effect or a career-stage effect?
assumptions_explicit: The paper is conceptual; no empirical data are collected or reported.
The paper must combine workplace ethics and Generation Z in a non-saturated way.
One or two established theories must ground the model.
No more than 5-6 propositions; no more than 3-4 constructs per variable.
assumptions_inferred: A theory-development article in the style of management/OB conceptual journals is the intended genre (inferred from the requested structure and the 'senior management researcher' framing).
No target journal was named, so a generic single-column author-year layout is acceptable.
constraints: Proposal mode (no numbers, no fabricated findings); every citation real and verified; figures limited to one conceptual model diagram.
retrieval_query: ideological psychological contract breach employee ethical voice channel internal versus external whistleblowing social media Generation Z cohort versus career stage
